content.title: About
content.content: Banana split is a classic dessert made of a banana sliced lengthwise, topped with scoops of ice cream (usually vanilla, chocolate and strawberry), whipped cream, chocolate sauce, nuts and a maraschino cherry. The treat is popular in the United States and many other countries.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The banana split was invented in 1904 at the Pharmacy drugstore in San Francisco.
Originally the dessert was presented as a "banana boat" with the banana as the hull and ice cream as the sails.
Local variations exist: in Japan green tea ice cream is used, in Italy a splash of amaretto is added.
Banana split often appears in advertising as a symbol of summer fun.
Vegan versions replace dairy ice cream with coconut or soy alternatives.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Bananas provide a good amount of potassium, which supports heart and muscle function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Bananas contain vitamin B6, important for protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: The fiber in bananas aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Antioxidants in berries and sauce
items.content: Cherries and chocolate sauce supply polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Protein from ice cream
items.content: Dairy‑based ice cream adds a modest amount of protein to the dessert.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The combination of ice cream, sauce and cherry makes the dessert very sweet, which can raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Traditional banana split contains dairy; lactose‑intolerant individuals should use lactose‑free alternatives.

items.title: Nut allergy
items.content: If nuts are added, they may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive people.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: Banana split is calorie‑rich; portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑loss diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the banana lengthwise, place it in a dish, add scoops of ice cream, drizzle chocolate sauce, top with whipped cream, nuts and a cherry. Fresh berries or a sprinkle of cinnamon can be added for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Serve a banana split immediately. If you need to store components, keep ice cream frozen and the banana refrigerated, but it’s best to assemble the dessert right before serving to prevent the banana from browning.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken patty, breaded is a ready‑to‑cook product made from minced chicken breast formed into a round patty and coated with a crispy breadcrumb crust. It is convenient for quick frying or baking and is suitable for both home and commercial kitchens.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken patties are a staple in fast‑food menus, especially in burgers and sandwiches.
The breading often contains herbs, spices, and seasoned crumbs for extra flavor.
The product is usually sold in vacuum‑sealed packs to extend shelf life.
Chicken is one of the most affordable sources of high‑quality protein, and the breading adds a satisfying crunch.
In many countries, chicken patties are used as a lower‑fat alternative to beef patties.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken provides all essential amino acids needed for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with beef patties, chicken versions typically contain less saturated fat.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B6 and B12 support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of selenium
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: Chicken meat is quickly digested, making it suitable for light or diet meals.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The breading is often salted; people monitoring sodium intake should watch portion size.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Improper storage can lead to growth of Salmonella; always follow use‑by dates and keep refrigerated.

items.title: Monosodium glutamate (MSG)
items.content: Some breading recipes include MSG, which may cause sensitivity in certain consumers.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: The patty can be pan‑fried with a little oil, baked in a preheated oven at 180 °C for 20‑25 minutes, or cooked in an air fryer. Let the patty come to room temperature before cooking for even heat distribution.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at +2…+4 °C in the original packaging for up to 5 days after opening. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 3 months. Before use, check for off‑odors or discoloration.

pasta-whole-grain-with-tomato-based-sauc.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Tomato Sauce, Seafood and Vegetables, Ready‑to‑Heat

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pasta with a tomato‑based sauce, seafood (shrimp, mussels) and added vegetables (bell pepper, zucchini, carrot) is a ready‑to‑heat meal that only needs warming. The combination of fiber‑rich pasta, flavorful sauce and marine protein makes it a balanced, nutritious option.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain pasta provides more fiber and micronutrients than refined‑wheat pasta.
Tomato sauce is rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that supports heart health.
Seafood is an excellent source of omega‑3 fatty acids, beneficial for brain function.
The vegetables retain most of their vitamins thanks to the quick cooking process.
The dish is designed for microwave or stovetop heating in 3–5 minutes.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole grain pasta helps regulate digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Complete protein source
items.content: Seafood combined with whole grain pasta supplies all essential amino acids.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes and vitamins from vegetables combat free radicals.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Seafood provides beneficial polyunsaturated fats that support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The meal contains vitamin C, vitamin A, iron and magnesium, important for immunity and energy.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: People allergic to fish or shellfish may react; always check the ingredient list.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauce and seafood can contribute notable sodium; monitor portion size if you watch blood pressure.

items.title: Heat handling
items.content: Overheating may dry out the pasta; follow the heating instructions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the meal in the microwave (2–3 minutes) or on the stove, stirring halfway. Serve immediately; optionally garnish with fresh basil or grated Parmesan.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0 °C–4 °C and consume within 5 days after opening. Freezing is not recommended as it may alter the texture of the seafood.

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of lean pork, carrots, broccoli and dark‑green leafy vegetables (spinach, kale, Swiss chard). It is prepared without potatoes or sauce, making it low‑calorie and nutrient‑dense.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pork is a rich source of high‑quality protein and vitamin B12.
Broccoli contains sulforaphane, a compound with antioxidant properties.
Carrots are high in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Dark‑green leafy greens provide vitamin K, essential for blood clotting.
Omitting potatoes and sauce reduces simple carbohydrates and added fats.

items.title: Supports muscle mass
items.content: Pork protein aids growth and repair of muscle tissue.

items.title: Boosts immunity
items.content: B‑vitamins and zinc in pork help maintain immune function.

items.title: Eye health
items.content: Beta‑carotene from carrots is converted to vitamin A, vital for vision.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Sulforaphane from broccoli and polyphenols from leafy greens combat free radicals.

items.title: Bone support
items.content: Vitamin K and calcium from leafy greens contribute to bone mineralization.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Some cuts of pork can be high in saturated fat; choose lean portions.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Pork should be cooked to an internal temperature of at least 71 °C to eliminate salmonella and trichinella.

items.title: Meat protein allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may be allergic to pork proteins.

items.title: Interaction with medication
items.content: High vitamin K levels can affect the efficacy of anticoagulant drugs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, slicing the pork into thin strips and mixing with boiled or lightly sautéed vegetables. Optionally add a splash of lemon juice or fresh herbs for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to at least 74 °C before consumption.
